3.1.4 Temperature spreads and limb darkening

A solid blackbox may have a single surface temperature, but the thermal radiation of a diffuse blackbox should have a spread in temperatures, because the temperature of an atmosphere increases with optical depth. A line of sight into a blackbox’s atmosphere passes through layers with different temperatures, although radiation from below the photosphere is mostly absorbed. For these reasons, a diffuse blackbox should display limb darkening, as lines of sight passing obliquely through the edges of the blackbox go through more matter per unit depth.

The temperature spread in the thermal emission alters the shape of the blackbox’s spectrum, if the blackbox is significantly hotter than the CMB. These differences show up in the peak of the excess spectrum and the Wien exponential tail, where the shape depends critically on temperature. But when observing at low frequencies, the thermal emission from each layer of the blackbox’s atmosphere is well-approximated by a Rayleigh-Jeans tail. The observed emission spectrum, as a weighted sum of these tails, should also have the characteristic Fν∝ν2proportional-tosubscript𝐹𝜈superscript𝜈2F_{\nu}\propto\nu^{2} shape. Only the amount and the angular distribution of the emission is altered because of limb darkening at low frequencies.

A cold blackbox (Δ​Tobs≪TCMBmuch-less-thanΔsubscript𝑇obssubscript𝑇CMB\Delta T_{\rm obs}\ll T_{\rm CMB}) also displays limb darkening of a sort, with the excess temperatures increasing deeper in the atmosphere, but the total temperature remains close to TCMBsubscript𝑇CMBT_{\rm CMB} for all lines of sight. This can be understood readily for a purely grey atmosphere in the blackbox. Then, radiative transfer of energy through the blackbox is characterized by a diffusion equation of the form ∇2u=0superscript∇2𝑢0\nabla^{2}u=0, where u𝑢u is the bolometric radiation energy density. This equation is linear in u𝑢u, so the radiation field can be separated into a uniform background uCMBsubscript𝑢CMBu_{\rm CMB} from the CMB and the excess radiation uintsubscript𝑢intu_{\rm int} from the blackbox’s internal luminosity. The dependence of uintsubscript𝑢intu_{\rm int} on optical depth is the same for hot and cold blackboxes; thus the CMB has no effect on the angular distribution of bolometric excess flux for a grey atmosphere. The shape of the excess flux spectrum from a cold blackbox is not affected by limb darkening, since it is the same for all Δ​Tobs≪TCMB​(0)much-less-thanΔsubscript𝑇obssubscript𝑇CMB0\Delta T_{\rm obs}\ll T_{\rm CMB}(0) (equation 3.1.2), and thus for each layer above the photosphere of the blackbox.

3.2. Transparency of blackboxes to non-thermal emission

A blackbox is opaque to its internal thermal radiation, in microwaves and possibly infrared, optical, and ultraviolet light. That still leaves low frequency radio, X-rays, and gamma rays as potential messengers from the interior of the blackbox, as well as particles like neutrinos. If aliens generate these forms of radiation within the blackboxes, they may still attempt to capture and process them, just like starlight.

Normal star-forming galaxies typically emit only a tiny fraction of their bolometric power through non-thermal mechanisms. The GHz synchrotron luminosity of a star-forming galaxy is only about a millionth of the infrared luminosity, for example (Yun et al., 2001). It is probably more advantageous to extract energy from the waste heat by building another layer around the blackbox and harnessing the temperature difference between the new, colder surface and the interior. Yet, harvesting non-thermal radiation may be easier since it does not require working with small temperature differences. Or, the occupants of a blackbox may try to stop non-thermal radiation simply to hide their activities or some other reason.

Radio emission can be absorbed quite efficiently with dipole antennas, similar to those that might be used to absorb the thermal radiation of a blackbox. I showed in Section 2.3 that the mass of an opaque dipole cloud does not depend on the wavelength at low frequencies – the effective area of the antenna increases as the square of its length, while the cross-section must also increase as the square of its length to avoid Ohmic losses. The dipole mass cloud grows proportionally to the number of decades of photon frequency that are stopped. Still, doubling the total mass of a dipole cloud should still be allowed in the mass budget of a galaxy if carbon nanotube antennas are used. For MHz radio waves, half-wavelength dipole antennas need to be kilometers long. Yet antennas that are hundreds of meters tall are used on the Earth for transmitting radio. Furthermore, interstellar space is a much gentler environment than the Earth, with negligible gravity, pressure, and temperature; building big antennas and setting them free in the ISM may work fine.

There is no obvious clever solution like dipole antennas for absorbing harder X-rays and gamma rays. The optical properties of a material depend on structures that are smaller than the wavelength of a photon; when the wavelength of a photon is smaller than an atom, only chemistry and nuclear physics matters. Hard ultraviolet light and soft X-rays are efficiently absorbed by the photoelectric effect in ISM hydrogen. But beyond a few keV, a blackbox can only be opaque if it is Compton thick, with a column density of order ΣC≈25​kg m−2subscriptΣ𝐶25superscriptkg m2\Sigma_{C}\approx 25\ \textrm{kg\ m}^{-2} (e.g., Olive et al., 2015). The amount of mass required to make a 10 kpc wide blackbox Compton thick, 4​π​Rbox2​ΣC4𝜋superscriptsubscript𝑅box2subscriptΣ𝐶4\pi R_{\rm box}^{2}\Sigma_{C}, exceeds the baryonic content of a galaxy:

Mbox≳1.5×1013​M⊙​(Rbox10​kpc)2​(Σ25​kg m−2).greater-than-or-equivalent-tosubscript𝑀box1.5superscript1013subscriptMdirect-productsuperscriptsubscript𝑅box10kpc2Σ25superscriptkg m2M_{\rm box}\gtrsim 1.5\times 10^{13}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot}\left(\frac{R_{\rm box}}{10\ \textrm{kpc}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{\Sigma}{25\ \textrm{kg\ m}^{-2}}\right). (51)

The situation is much worse still for high energy gamma rays, which are typically stopped by columns of ∼1000​kg m−2similar-toabsent1000superscriptkg m2\sim 1000\ \textrm{kg\ m}^{-2} (Olive et al., 2015).

3.3. Blackboxes colder than the CMB?

Wright et al. (2014b) brings up the possibility that cosmic engineers are not bound by the conservation of energy as we understand it. If they can summon astronomical amounts of energy, that can increase the waste heat. As Wright et al. (2014b) points out in the context of Chilly Ways, the excess power conjured against the First Law of Thermodynamics cannot be vastly greater than the typical luminosity of a galaxy, or else it would have been seen with WISE. Similar considerations apply for blackboxes; they would have been detected by Planck and earlier surveys. If the First Law of Thermodynamics does not hold, then perhaps aliens destroy astronomical amounts of energy. Then waste heat is reduced or eliminated, and it is harder to see a blackbox or a Chilly Way.

Instead of energy conservation, what if aliens know a way around the Second Law of Thermodynamics, unlikely as that is? In the worst case from an observer’s point of view (but not the aliens’), energy is continuously recycled and never released as waste heat. As far as searches in the microwave and infrared regions are concerned, it might as well be as if the aliens are not there. But there is another possibility – the blackbox (or Chilly Way) can be refrigerated until it is much colder than the CMB. Then the aliens can harness the power contained within the CMB itself. For a blackbox the size of a galaxy, this power is almost of the same magnitude as the starlight itself.

Even within the laws of thermodynamics, a refrigerated blackbox is possible if it is opaque to low energy neutrinos or gravitational waves. The temperature of the cosmic neutrino background from the Big Bang is expected to be only 1.95 K (Egan & Lineweaver, 2010). A blackbox could potentially use the CMB as a hot reservoir and the neutrino background as a cold reservoir and extract useful work. Just as the EBL heats a blackbox slightly over the CMB, the diffuse supernova neutrino background may heat a neutrino-opaque blackbox. The energy density in the supernova neutrino background is probably comparable to that of the EBL (Beacom, 2010), so this heating is at most a few hundredths of a Kelvin, compared to a potential cooling of a few tenths of a Kelvin. The relic gravitational wave background, if there is one, is thought to be even colder, at less than 1 K (Egan & Lineweaver, 2010), providing another possible cold reservoir. Of course, a galaxy-sized shroud that can absorb neutrinos and especially gravitational waves defies our knowledge of material physics.

A very large black hole would also appear colder than the CMB, if it was large enough to cast a detectable shadow, and would still be allowed by thermodynamics. Rich galaxy clusters contain about 1015​M⊙superscript1015subscriptMdirect-product10^{15}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of matter. If it was all fed into a single black hole, the hole would grow to have a Schwarzschild radius of about 100 pc. The shadow would then have a flux deficit of ∼1​mJysimilar-toabsent1mJy\sim 1\ \textrm{mJy} at 150 GHz if the hole was 100 Mpc away. This is too small to be detected by Planck, although the South Pole Telescope might detect the deficit.

A blackbox that is colder than the CMB should appear to have a negative excess flux in the microwaves. In fact, this is exactly what some surveys are looking for – galaxy clusters appear to have negative flux at low frequencies thanks to the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (Sunyaev & Zeldovich, 1972). But the Compton effect responsible for the Sunyaev-Zeldovich phenomenon merely boosts the energy of photons to slightly higher energy; the missing flux appears at high frequencies. Thus, these galaxy clusters appear hotter at high frequencies (Sunyaev & Zeldovich, 1972). A refrigerated blackbox appears as a negative source at all frequencies.

The CMB does not have exactly the same temperature in every direction, but is slightly cooler in a few parts of the sky than others. A refrigerated blackbox appears like an extreme temperature anomaly, with a magnitude of order a K instead of a few dozen μ​K𝜇K\mu\textrm{K}. Clearly, if any such blackboxes existed and were resolved in the sky by Planck, it would have been noticed by now in searches for non-Gaussian anomalies. Even if it was just the size of the Milky Way, and unresolved, the negative flux from the blackbox would be of order −1​Jy1Jy-1\ \textrm{Jy}, easily noticed by Planck and Sunyaev-Zeldovich surveys (equation 41). Thus, there are probably no large, refrigerated blackboxes.

4. Blackboxes Don’t Exist

4.1. Which surveys to use?

The thermal emission of a blackbox comes out in radio, microwave, and infrared bands. Infrared surveys can be useful for hot blackboxes, just like they are for Dyson spheres (Griffith et al., 2015), but they are essentially useless for cold blackboxes with Tobs≈TCMB​(0)subscript𝑇obssubscript𝑇CMB0T_{\rm obs}\approx T_{\rm CMB}(0). All (conventional) blackboxes should emit microwave thermal emission, since they are at least as hot as the CMB, but all-sky microwave surveys tend to be relatively shallow. Finally, although blackboxes are much fainter at GHz radio frequencies, a radio survey might pick up their emission anyway, much like how radio telescopes can study the extended photospheres of giant stars (Reid & Menten, 1997). Fortunately, there are now many all-sky and large field surveys for all three, which I list in Table 4. But which of these is most constraining?

This depends on whether one knows where to look. A survey reaches some minimum flux Fνminsubscriptsuperscript𝐹min𝜈F^{\rm min}_{\nu} and covers some solid angle on the sky ΩΩ\Omega. There are three possibilities to consider.

First, what if one wanted to catalog all the blackboxes in some well-defined region of space, like a given galaxy cluster? Then, it does not matter if the survey is wide-field or not, as long as it covers the target region. The effectiveness of the survey depends only on the ratio of the expected flux to the minimum flux, which can be parameterized by

Ωchar−1=IνexcessFνmin.superscriptsubscriptΩchar1subscriptsuperscript𝐼excess𝜈subscriptsuperscript𝐹min𝜈\Omega_{\rm char}^{-1}=\frac{I^{\rm excess}_{\nu}}{F^{\rm min}_{\nu}}. (52)

A blackbox that covers a solid angle ΩblackboxsubscriptΩblackbox\Omega_{\rm blackbox} on the sky is detectable if Ωblackbox​Ωchar−1≳1greater-than-or-equivalent-tosubscriptΩblackboxsuperscriptsubscriptΩchar11\Omega_{\rm blackbox}\Omega_{\rm char}^{-1}\gtrsim 1.

What if one wanted to construct a luminosity-selected catalog of blackboxes, or to measure the fraction of galaxies sealed in blackboxes in the local Universe? Blackboxes with the necessary luminosity are visible out to some comoving distance Rmaxsubscript𝑅maxR_{\rm max}. The survey effectiveness is measured by how much comoving volume it examines: 𝒱=(Ω/3)​Dmax3𝒱Ω3superscriptsubscript𝐷max3{\cal V}=(\Omega/3)D_{\rm max}^{3}, where ΩΩ\Omega is the solid angle covered by the survey. If the blackboxes are relatively faint, then Dmaxsubscript𝐷maxD_{\rm max} is small compared to cosmological scales and has the form Dmax=R¯​π/Ωcharsubscript𝐷max¯𝑅𝜋subscriptΩcharD_{\rm max}=\overline{R}\sqrt{\pi/\Omega_{\rm char}}, where R¯¯𝑅\overline{R} is a reference radius of a blackbox. The sampled comoving volume is then proportional to

𝒱=Ω​R¯33​(πΩchar)3/2.𝒱Ωsuperscript¯𝑅33superscript𝜋subscriptΩchar32{\cal V}=\frac{\Omega\overline{R}^{3}}{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{\Omega_{\rm char}}\right)^{3/2}. (53)

On the other hand, if the blackboxes are very bright, they can be visible anywhere in the Universe. This is actually true for blackboxes that contain rich galaxy clusters. Then, Dmaxsubscript𝐷maxD_{\rm max} has no dependence on the survey sensitivity. The only quantity that matters is the survey area ΩΩ\Omega.

I calculated these figures of merit for some radio, microwave, and infrared surveys and have listed them in Table 4. The quantities differ for cold blackboxes, with a flux given by equation 3.1.2, and hot blackboxes, with a Rayleigh-Jeans spectrum (equation 40). Of the all-sky surveys, the Planck 217 GHz PCCS2 catalog is the best for cold blackboxes. Other Planck bands, from 100 to 353 GHz, have a respectable sensitivity too. But the South Pole Telescope Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SPT-SZ) survey has a much greater depth still at the cost of survey area; it is much better at finding smaller, fainter blackboxes. Although not anywhere near as sensitive as the microwave surveys, the NVSS (NRAO VLA Sky Survey) catalog still has an effective reach of millions of Mpc3superscriptMpc3\textrm{Mpc}^{3}, despite being at 1.4 GHz. If a blackbox were found, a radio telescope could check whether it has a thermal spectrum out to long wavelengths. The Australia Telescope 20 GHz (AT20G) survey is about as effective at Planck’s 30 GHz channel. Furthermore, radio interferometers have a much better angular resolution than Planck, and are better at measuring the size of a blackbox. Cold blackboxes emit no detectable infrared flux, and so are missed by the infrared surveys in Table 4.

Infrared surveys are extremely effective at finding hot blackboxes. When searching for blackboxes with a fixed high temperature and radius, AKARI’s far infrared (FIR) survey has a volume reach that is thousands of times better than Planck. The volume reach of WISE is about a billion times times that of Planck. The apparent weakness of Planck comes about because at high temperatures, very little of the luminosity comes out in microwaves, since Fν∝ν2proportional-tosubscript𝐹𝜈superscript𝜈2F_{\nu}\propto\nu^{2}. If we fix the luminosity only and compare the reach of Planck for cold blackboxes and the reach of WISE for blackboxes with Tobssubscript𝑇obsT_{\rm obs} of a few hundred K, the survey volumes are roughly the same. This demonstrates that WISE is effective for finding classical Dyson spheres and Chilly Ways. All of these surveys are all-sky, so we do not have to worry that a blackbox is hiding outside of their survey field. But these figures assume that the blackboxes are hot, with x=h​ν/(kB​Tobs)≲1𝑥ℎ𝜈subscript𝑘𝐵subscript𝑇obsless-than-or-similar-to1x=h\nu/(k_{B}T_{\rm obs})\lesssim 1. The FIR surveys are useful only if Tobs≳20​Kgreater-than-or-equivalent-tosubscript𝑇obs20KT_{\rm obs}\gtrsim 20\ \textrm{K} and WISE is useful only if Tobs≳50​Kgreater-than-or-equivalent-tosubscript𝑇obs50KT_{\rm obs}\gtrsim 50\ \textrm{K}.

4.2. Results from the Planck Catalog of Compact Sources

I concentrated my efforts on looking for blackboxes in the PCCS2 catalog (Ade et al., 2015). Although it is not optimal in all cases, the Planck PCCS2 survey performs fairly well over a wide range of blackbox sizes and luminosities. The effectiveness of each channel is shown in Figure 3. In addition, the spectral slope of blackboxes is confined to a relatively narrow range at low frequency, and can be used to select candidate blackboxes. Finally, the PCCS2 also has only a few thousand sources at most in each band, so it can be examined quickly. I restrict my search to the primary PCCS2 catalog and do not include those in the “excluded” PCCS2E catalogs covering regions contaminated by Galactic dust. This greatly reduces the number of sources at the cost of sacrificing some sky area at high frequencies.

I matched sources in each pair of channels in order to check their spectral index. Each source in the first channel was provisionally matched to the source in the second channel that was nearest to its position. The match was considered valid if (1) the potential matches were less than 30 arcminutes apart (the approximate size of the 30 GHz Planck beam; Ade et al. 2015) and (2) the match was consistent both ways – that is, the nearest source in the first channel to the potential match in the second channel was the original source. Generally, those sources that matched had positions consistent to within an arcminute or two, and it was rare that a source in the second channel was the closest to one in the first channel but not the other way around.

For the photometry, I used the DETFLUX values listed in the PCCS2, which are the flux levels derived by the PCCS2 detection pipeline (Ade et al., 2015). These were measured under the assumption that the sources are pointlike. This is basically true for galaxy-sized blackboxes, which cover a solid angle of ∼0.3​(Rbox/10​kpc)2​(DA/100​Mpc)−2similar-toabsent0.3superscriptsubscript𝑅box10kpc2superscriptsubscript𝐷𝐴100Mpc2\sim 0.3\ (R_{\rm box}/10\ \textrm{kpc})^{2}(D_{A}/100\ \textrm{Mpc})^{-2} square arcminutes, compared to the 100 GHz beam of about 100 square arcminutes (Ade et al., 2015). The DETFLUX values have the smallest uncertainties, minimizing the errors in the spectral slope. I do also consider the other three photometry methods, but the uncertainties in those measurements are often as big as the fluxes themselves. Many sources that simply have poor flux determinations pass the cut on α𝛼\alpha, diluting those results.

I then calculated the spectral slope of the source between the two channels. The uncertainty in the spectral slope was calculated according to

σα=(σ1F1)2+(σ2F2)2/ln⁡(ν2ν1),subscript𝜎𝛼superscriptsubscript𝜎1subscript𝐹12superscriptsubscript𝜎2subscript𝐹22subscript𝜈2subscript𝜈1\sigma_{\alpha}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_{1}}{F_{1}}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\sigma_{2}}{F_{2}}\right)^{2}}\big{/}\ln\left(\frac{\nu_{2}}{\nu_{1}}\right), (54)

where F1subscript𝐹1F_{1} and F2subscript𝐹2F_{2} were the fluxes in the first and second channels, and σ1subscript𝜎1\sigma_{1} and σ2subscript𝜎2\sigma_{2} were the flux uncertainties in these channels. The matched sources were selected if αmin≤α+2​σαsubscript𝛼min𝛼2subscript𝜎𝛼\alpha_{\rm min}\leq\alpha+2\sigma_{\alpha} and α−2​σα≤2.0𝛼2subscript𝜎𝛼2.0\alpha-2\sigma_{\alpha}\leq 2.0, where the minimum spectral slope αminsubscript𝛼min\alpha_{\rm min} is that of a cold blackbox (equation 49).

The number of sources that pass these cuts for each pair of channels is listed in Table 5. At high frequencies, the spectral slope constraints are not very powerful, and hundreds of sources pass. But at low frequencies, relatively few sources have slopes in the narrow range. In fact, there are some pairs of channels that select no sources. In other words, there are no blackboxes bright enough to be detected by Planck at both of these frequencies – even though the reach of Planck includes millions of Mpc3superscriptMpc3\textrm{Mpc}^{3}.

When I consider the other photometry sets in the PCCS2, the power of the cuts is somewhat weakened because of the greater uncertainties in α𝛼\alpha. The GAUSSFLUX photometry method was designed to handle extended sources by fitting a surface brightness profile to the maps. I find that no sources are selected for ν1=subscript𝜈1absent\nu_{1}= 70 GHz and ν2=subscript𝜈2absent\nu_{2}= 143, 217, or 353 GHz. In contrast, with the APERFLUX photometry, the only pair of channels with no selected sources is ν1=subscript𝜈1absent\nu_{1}= 30 GHz and ν2=subscript𝜈2absent\nu_{2}= 217 GHz; with the PSFFLUX photometry, the same pair of frequencies leads to 4 selected sources, the fewest of any pair. The APERFLUX and PSFFLUX photometry would lead to the poorest results if accepted, since the low frequency channels are so insensitive (as in Figure 3).

4.2.1 The nine (refuted) candidates spanning 100 and 217 GHz

The 100 GHz channel is more sensitive than the lower frequency channels with no matched sources. As listed in Table 5, only nine sources pass all of the cuts with ν1=subscript𝜈1absent\nu_{1}= 100 GHz and ν2=subscript𝜈2absent\nu_{2}= 217 GHz. Checking these nine is a very quick matter, and one unlikely to produce false positives. These nine sources are listed in Table 6.

Three of the sources (NGC 253, NGC 891, and M82) are nearby infrared-bright starburst galaxies (Sanders et al., 2003). NGC 1068 is mostly powered by its Seyfert nucleus, although it also has a prominent starburst region (Telesco et al., 1984). The 100 GHz luminosity of these galaxies is a combination of synchrotron emission from cosmic ray electrons, free-free emission from H II regions, and thermal emission from dust (Williams & Bower, 2010). The 217 GHz luminosity is mostly the thermal glow of dust heated by starlight in the starburst (and Seyfert) regions (Williams & Bower, 2010; Peel et al., 2011). It is possible that these starburst regions are opaque to their own FIR radiation (c. f., Thompson et al., 2005), making them natural blackboxes of a sort, but they are transparent at the millimeter wavelengths considered here. This is demonstrated by the positive curvature in their microwave spectra, in contrast to the negative curvature expected of a blackbox spectrum.

Another of the sources, NGC 460, is also associated with intense star formation. This open star cluster is contained within the N84 H II region in the Small Magellanic Cloud (Henize, 1956; Davies et al., 1976; Testor & Lortet, 1987). The fluxes at 217 GHz and above fall along an approximate Rayleigh-Jeans tail, consistent with dust. At lower frequencies, the spectrum is flat in Fνsubscript𝐹𝜈F_{\nu}, possibly indicating free-free emission. Thus, NGC 460 has a positive curvature in its millimeter spectrum and is not a natural blackbox at these frequencies.

Two more of the sources are coincident with the molecular clouds [CB88] 28 (Clemens & Barvainis, 1988) and Dobashi 6193 (Dobashi, 2011). The positions of the sources at 100 and 217 GHz are separated by 7.′arcminute\farcm for Dobashi 6193 and almost half a degree for [CB] 28, probably because the clouds are part of large dusty complexes on the sky. Both dust complexes are obvious sources in AKARI images, and their obscuration is easily seen in DSS2 (Digitized Sky Survey) images. Planck’s photometry is unreliable at frequencies above 217 GHz in these regions, but the spectra of these sources appears to be roughly flat at 100 GHz for [CB] 28 and then rising for both nebulas.

The eighth source is the carbon star CW Leo (IRC+10216), one of the most brilliant stars in the sky in the MIR (Becklin et al., 1969). Dusty, massive circumstellar shells surround the star, effectively shrouding it in a natural stellar-scale blackbox (Toombs et al., 1972). The Planck photometry indicates a Rayleigh-Jeans tail (Figure 4). That is in line with other measurements, spanning the radio to the MIR, although the spectrum may start to diverge from α=2𝛼2\alpha=2 at millimeter and radio wavelengths as the shells become transparent (Sahai et al., 1989; Griffin, 1990). CW Leo and similar stars are known to be potential false positives in searches for Dyson spheres (Carrigan, 2009), much like how it turns up here in a blackbox search.

The last source is harder to identify, but it is in the vicinity of the Mira variable star UW CMi (Smak & Preston, 1965) and a filament of Galactic dust. The source is faintly detected at 100 GHz, but not in the more sensitive 143 GHz channel (Figure 4). Then, starting at 217 GHz, it has a Rayleigh-Jeans spectrum (blue line in Figure 4), if the PCCS2E photometry is included. On the Planck maps, the source appears faint and unresolved at 100 GHz (Figure 5). At 217 GHz and higher, it is clear that a Galactic dust filament runs through the region. There is also what appears to be an unresolved point source (Figure 5). Maybe the point source is just a knot or projection effect of the Galactic dust filament, but Mira variables like UW CMi occasionally are obscured by dusty shells, showing up as infrared and radio sources (Bedijn, 1987; Reid & Menten, 1997). Something identified as UW CMi (=07451611+0110558, IRAS 07426+0118) is in fact included in the COBE (Cosmic Background Explorer) DIRBE (Diffuse Infrared Background Experiment) point source catalog, although the photometry is only reliable at 4.9μ​m𝜇m\ \mu\textrm{m} and bluer (Smith et al., 2004).

Whatever this remaining source is, it is probably not a blackbox. If it were, it should be brighter at 143 GHz than at 100 GHz. This is seen from the red curve in Figure 4, which is the cold blackbox flux spectrum normalized to run through the 100 GHz point. A hot blackbox would be even brighter at 143 GHz than a cold blackbox. The nature of the 100 GHz detection remains unclear, though.

4.3. The significance of the null results

My quick look through the Planck source catalog revealed no blackboxes. There is, of course, plenty of room for improving the methods I used, by investigating every source in the catalog at all frequencies and eliminating those with known counterparts. The 100 GHz band is by no means the most sensitive of Planck’s channels to blackboxes, as seen in Figure 3. But even this cursory search’s null result is remarkable. As seen in Table 4, the 100 GHz band of Planck has a reach that includes about a Gpc3superscriptGpc3\textrm{Gpc}^{3} for Milky Way-containing blackboxes.

A more precise bound depends on the size of the blackbox and its excess luminosity. The parameter space ruled out by Planck’s 100 GHz source catalog is shown in Figure 6. Big and bright blackboxes are ruled out. The bound at a given distance asymptotes to a constant excess luminosity when the blackbox is big – it generally does not matter whether it is 1 Mpc or 10 Mpc wide, if the excess luminosity remains constant. The excess heating that is provided by the EBL sets a minimum luminosity, excluding the possibility of big but dim blackboxes. Thus, Planck is already effective at ruling out cluster-sized blackboxes, for example, even if the entities inside wish to conserve energy. When the blackbox is small (and therefore hot), the bound has the asymptotic form of Lexcess∝Rbox−6proportional-tosubscript𝐿excesssuperscriptsubscript𝑅box6L_{\rm excess}\propto R_{\rm box}^{-6} – there is a weak dependence on the internal luminosity, but Planck is not sensitive to blackboxes that are only a parsec wide even if Lexcess≈1014​L⊙subscript𝐿excesssuperscript1014subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm excess}\approx 10^{14}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} that are a few hundred Mpc away.

From Figure 6, it is clear that my null result rules out much of the relevant parameter space for blackboxes out to Gpc distances. Specifically, blackboxes that are brighter than a trillion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} are ruled out to a comoving distance of 1.5 Gpc (z=0.37𝑧0.37z=0.37) as long as they are at least 10 kpc in radius. Trillion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} luminosities are attained in ultra-luminous infrared galaxies, active galactic nuclei, and galaxy clusters. Galaxy clusters shrouded in blackboxes are detectable out to much further still, 2.6 Gpc (z=0.71𝑧0.71z=0.71) if εEBL=0subscript𝜀EBL0\varepsilon_{\rm EBL}=0 and 7.3 Gpc (z=3.9𝑧3.9z=3.9) if εEBL=0.05subscript𝜀EBL0.05\varepsilon_{\rm EBL}=0.05. But the lookback time at z=0.7𝑧0.7z=0.7 includes almost half of the Universe’s history. Unless some aliens evolved early in the Universe’s history, there are no such blackboxes anywhere in the observable Universe.

The bounds on blackboxes with smaller luminosities more like those of present-day galaxies remain impressive. When the excess luminosity is 100 billion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} and the radius is bigger than about 10 kpc, blackboxes should be detected by Planck’s 100 GHz channel out to 820 Mpc (z=0.19𝑧0.19z=0.19). The Milky Way is slightly dimmer than this, with a total luminosity of around 65 billion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} (Strong et al., 2010), but if it were shrouded in a blackbox, it would have been detected out 720 Mpc. Even something only as bright as one of the Magellanic Clouds, with a billion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot}, would have been seen if it was within 140 Mpc.

I find the number of galaxies within the survey volume by integrating galaxy mass functions:

Nreach=∫Ω100−217​DC,max33​d​nd​M⋆​𝑑M⋆.subscript𝑁reachsubscriptΩ100217superscriptsubscript𝐷Cmax33𝑑𝑛𝑑subscript𝑀⋆differential-dsubscript𝑀⋆N_{\rm reach}=\int\frac{\Omega_{100-217}D_{\rm C,max}^{3}}{3}\frac{dn}{dM_{\star}}dM_{\star}. (55)

I used the mass function number densities d​n/d​M⋆𝑑𝑛𝑑subscript𝑀⋆dn/dM_{\star} from Baldry et al. (2012) for z<0.2𝑧0.2z<0.2 and Muzzin et al. (2013) for z≥0.2𝑧0.2z\geq 0.2. The maximum comoving distance a blackbox is detectable DC,maxsubscript𝐷CmaxD_{\rm C,max} depends on the internal galaxy luminosity. I calculate these by assuming a bolometric stellar mass-to-luminosity ratio of 2 M⊙/L⊙subscriptMdirect-productsubscriptLdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot}/\textrm{L}_{\odot} for red galaxies (from the models of Maraston 1998 and Vázquez & Leitherer 2005 for a 10 Gyr old stellar population, adjusted for IMF) and 0.5 M⊙/L⊙subscriptMdirect-productsubscriptLdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot}/\textrm{L}_{\odot} for blue galaxies (the B𝐵B-band mass-to-light ratio quoted in Baldry et al. 2012; naively extrapolating the values given in Leitherer et al. 1999 for a continuously star-forming population to 10 Gyr gives ∼similar-to\sim0.4 M⊙/L⊙subscriptMdirect-productsubscriptLdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot}/\textrm{L}_{\odot}). The blackbox radius is assumed to be 10 kpc. The PCCS2 only covers a part of the sky at high frequencies because of possible contamination from the emission of Galactic dust. The Ω100−217subscriptΩ100217\Omega_{100-217} factor accounts for this; it is the solid angle covered in both the 100 GHz and 217 GHz catalogs. Table 4 lists how much of the sky is included in each channel. Since my search in Section 4.2.1 includes sources that are in both the 100 GHz and 217 GHz catalogs, the best possible solid angle covered by both is 65.9% if the 100 GHz exclusion area is contained entirely within the 217 GHz exclusion area, while the worst possible solid angle is 100−15.0−34.1=50.9%10015.034.1percent50.9100-15.0-34.1=50.9\%. It is clear from the maps in Ade et al. (2015) that the optimistic case is more accurate, so I use 65.9%.

A quantity more directly related to the number of inhabited planets is the stellar mass in these galaxies, since its unlikely that there are as many in small galaxies as in large galaxies:

Mreach=∫Ω100−217​DC,max33​M⋆​d​nd​M⋆​𝑑M⋆.subscript𝑀reachsubscriptΩ100217superscriptsubscript𝐷Cmax33subscript𝑀⋆𝑑𝑛𝑑subscript𝑀⋆differential-dsubscript𝑀⋆M_{\rm reach}=\int\frac{\Omega_{100-217}D_{\rm C,max}^{3}}{3}M_{\star}\frac{dn}{dM_{\star}}dM_{\star}. (56)

Baldry et al. (2012) uses a Chabrier initial mass function (IMF) for the stellar population, so that’s what I use as well. Zackrisson et al. (2016) estimates that there are about 1.5 terrestrial planets per M⊙subscriptMdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot} of stellar mass in the Universe for this IMF, mostly around M dwarfs. The number of terrestrial planets for F, G, and K class stars is much smaller at 0.064 per M⊙subscriptMdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot}. These rates allow me to estimate the number of terrestrial planets in the survey volume. Finally, I can derive an effective volume of the survey, Veff=Mreach/⟨ρ⋆⟩subscript𝑉effsubscript𝑀reachdelimited-⟨⟩subscript𝜌⋆V_{\rm eff}=M_{\rm reach}/\langle\rho_{\star}\rangle, from the average cosmic density of stars at z=0𝑧0z=0, ⟨ρ⋆⟩=2.3×108​M⊙​Mpc−3delimited-⟨⟩subscript𝜌⋆2.3superscript108subscriptMdirect-productsuperscriptMpc3\langle\rho_{\star}\rangle=2.3\times 10^{8}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot}\ \textrm{Mpc}^{-3} (Baldry et al., 2012).

From equation 55, I find that there are 3.0 million galaxies that would have been found in my search if they had been converted into blackboxes. These galaxies contain 1.8×1017​M⊙1.8superscript1017subscriptMdirect-product1.8\times 10^{17}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars. The contributions of galaxies of different masses to this limit (but not accounting for the smaller sky coverage at 217 GHz) are shown in Figure 7. The search is biased towards galaxies with ∼1011​M⊙similar-toabsentsuperscript1011subscriptMdirect-product\sim 10^{11}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars. This comes out to 2.6×10172.6superscript10172.6\times 10^{17} terrestrial planets within the surveyed galaxies, with 1.1×10161.1superscript10161.1\times 10^{16} terrestrial planets around F, G, and K stars. I calculate an effective volume of 0.98 Gpc3superscriptGpc3\textrm{Gpc}^{3}.

There are a few factors that weaken these constraints when setting actual upper bounds, but the basic point still stands. The PCCS2 is estimated to be 90% complete. For the sake of argument, suppose that the completeness fcompletesubscript𝑓completef_{\rm complete} in both the 100 GHz and 217 GHz channels together is 0.92=81%superscript0.92percent810.9^{2}=81\%. It is also possible that the null result is a fluke of Poisson statistics. The upper bound on the abundance of blackboxes is then

𝒜blackbox=N¯fcomplete​Nreach,subscript𝒜blackbox¯𝑁subscript𝑓completesubscript𝑁reach{\cal A}_{\rm blackbox}=\frac{\overline{N}}{f_{\rm complete}N_{\rm reach}}, (57)

where N¯¯𝑁\overline{N} is the largest average number of detections compatible with a null result at the desired confidence level. For a 95% confidence level, N¯=3.0¯𝑁3.0\overline{N}=3.0 (Olive et al., 2015). By combining the results of equation 55 with equation 57, I find that my search sets a 95% confidence level upper limit of 1.2×10−61.2superscript1061.2\times 10^{-6} on the frequency of blackboxes per galaxy, or less than one per 810,000 galaxies. There are roughly 4.8×1016​M⊙4.8superscript1016subscriptMdirect-product4.8\times 10^{16}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars expected in this many galaxies, with about 7.1×10167.1superscript10167.1\times 10^{16} terrestrial planets, 3.0×10153.0superscript10153.0\times 10^{15} of them around F, G, and K stars (Baldry et al., 2012; Zackrisson et al., 2016). In other words, less than one in seventy quadrillion terrestrial planets has been the home of blackbox-builders.

A more conservative limit is derived using the null detections for the 70 and 143 GHz catalogs using the GAUSSFLUX (and DETFLUX) photometry (Figure 8). These limits require replacing Ω100−217subscriptΩ100217\Omega_{100-217} with Ω70−143subscriptΩ70143\Omega_{70-143}, the fraction of the sky covered by the PCCS2 catalog at both 70 and 143 GHz, which is 85%. Then blackboxes are ruled out in 610,000 galaxies with 3.2×1016​M⊙3.2superscript1016subscriptMdirect-product3.2\times 10^{16}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars and 4.7×10164.7superscript10164.7\times 10^{16} terrestrial planets. These figures lead to a 95% confidence level upper limit of one blackbox per 166,000 galaxies that contain 8.5×1015​M⊙8.5superscript1015subscriptMdirect-product8.5\times 10^{15}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars and 1.3×10161.3superscript10161.3\times 10^{16} terrestrial planets. If I am even more conservative and only consider the null detections for the 30 and 217 GHz pair using the APERFLUX photometry, then my limits are about an order of magnitude times weaker than these values.

These results are favorable compared to other searches for extragalactic cosmic engineering. Most searches before Ĝ only included about a hundred galaxies, thousands of times fewer than the cold blackbox limit. Griffith et al. (2015) estimated that there were roughly 100,000 resolved galaxies in Ĝ, out of a possible 230,000 sources not close to the Galactic plane. This translates to a 95% confidence level upper limit of about 1 Chilly Way per 33,000 galaxies that captures at least 85% of the host’s starlight. The blackbox limit is twenty (four) times constraining for the DETFLUX (GAUSSFLUX) null results. From the lack of extragalactic cosmic engineers in the Milky Way, Olson (2015) constrained the abundance of expanding Type III+ societies to be ≲1​Gpc−3less-than-or-similar-toabsent1superscriptGpc3\lesssim 1\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}, depending on how fast they expand and when they evolved. Those values are in line with the null result presented here.

On a final note, the limits are far more powerful still on galaxy clusters shrouded in blackboxes (with Rbox=3​Mpcsubscript𝑅box3MpcR_{\rm box}=3\ \textrm{Mpc}). These can be detected out to z≥0.5𝑧0.5z\geq 0.5 in any of the low frequency channels of Planck. I estimate the number of galaxy clusters in the survey volume with the luminosity function fits of Bahcall (1979). Two cases are considered: rich galaxy clusters only with Lint≥1013​L⊙subscript𝐿intsuperscript1013subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm int}\geq 10^{13}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} using the fit for Abell clusters, and galaxy clusters and groups with Lint≥1012​L⊙subscript𝐿intsuperscript1012subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm int}\geq 10^{12}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} using the fit for single galaxies, groups, and clusters. As with red galaxies, I assume that the mass-to-light ratio is 2 M⊙/L⊙subscriptMdirect-productsubscriptLdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot}/\textrm{L}_{\odot}; although the luminosities are given for V-band, I assume that they are equal to the bolometric luminosity. The 70 and 143 GHz pair of channels is actually more constraining than 100 and 217 GHz, since they cover more of the sky (cluster blackboxes are still easily visible at 70 GHz, as seen in Figure 8). Only clusters with z≤0.5𝑧0.5z\leq 0.5 are included, but otherwise I ignore evolution effects.

As seen in Figure 7, more stellar mass resides in detectable galaxy clusters than in normal galaxies. There are roughly 30,000 rich clusters with 7.9×1017​M⊙7.9superscript1017subscriptMdirect-product7.9\times 10^{17}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars (95% confidence level limits: 1 in 8,200 rich clusters; 1 in 2.1×1017​M⊙2.1superscript1017subscriptMdirect-product2.1\times 10^{17}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars). Naively applying the cosmic planet abundance rate of Zackrisson et al. (2016), there are 1.2 quintillion planets in these clusters, of which, 50 quadrillion orbit F, G, and K stars (95% confidence level limits: 1 in 320 quadrillion terrestrial planets, 14 quadrillion around F, G, and K stars).

From the Bahcall (1979) luminosity function, there are about 700,000 galaxy cluster and groups with Lint≥1012​L⊙subscript𝐿intsuperscript1012subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm int}\geq 10^{12}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} out to z≥0.5𝑧0.5z\geq 0.5, almost all of which could have been detected in this survey. There is some weak dependence on εEBLsubscript𝜀EBL\varepsilon_{\rm EBL}, which affects the limits below 70 GHz; a 3 Mpc wide blackbox would be visible simply by re-radiating 5% of the incident EBL. In any case, there are about 3×1018​M⊙3superscript1018subscriptMdirect-product3\times 10^{18}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars with 5 quintillion planets (95% confidence level limits: 1 in 200,000 clusters and groups, 9×1017​M⊙9superscript1017subscriptMdirect-product9\times 10^{17}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars, and 1.4 quintillion planets).

About 1 in 5 stars at z≈0𝑧0z\approx 0 resides in a galaxy cluster666I derive this from the cosmic baryon density, derived from Ade et al. (2015), a fraction of 4% of baryons in ICM according to Shull et al. (2012), and an approximate mass ratio of 5 to 1 of ICM to stars in clusters with a few 1014​M⊙superscript1014subscriptMdirect-product10^{14}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of total mass (Gonzalez et al., 2013). The resulting average cluster stellar density is compared to the total value from Baldry et al. (2012). The Bahcall (1979) luminosity functions imply that ∼10%similar-toabsentpercent10\sim 10\% of stars reside in rich clusters with L≥1013​L⊙𝐿superscript1013subscriptLdirect-productL\geq 10^{13}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot}, but ∼60%similar-toabsentpercent60\sim 60\% are in groups and clusters with L≥1012​L⊙𝐿superscript1012subscriptLdirect-productL\geq 10^{12}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot}.; that is the appeal of limits on shrouded clusters. On the other hand, the amount of materials required may be prohibitive according to Section 2.3.1. Collecting the necessary materials from the ICM may take much longer than the age of the Universe too (Appendix F). Furthermore, it is possible that some constraints prevent intelligence from evolving in cluster environments, in analogy with the suggestion of a “galactic habitable zone” (Gonzalez et al., 2001). I therefore do not dwell on them too much, but their habitability and cosmic engineering potential may be worth exploring in more detail.

4.4. How to sharpen the null result with extant data

And yet the 100 GHz channel of Planck is not the most sensitive to blackboxes by any means (Figure 3).

Tighter limits are possible if we assume that none of the PCCS2 sources in any channel are blackboxes. Nothing like a blackbox has ever been reported by Planck or anyone else, so they are probably very rare, but to be sure each source should be identified and/or examined. Figure 9 shows the final sensitivity of Planck that is possible if there are no blackboxes in the PCCS2 catalogs. The PCCS2 should include any blackboxes with excess luminosity of at least 500 billion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} and radius greater than 10 kpc out to a comoving distance of 2.8 Gpc (z=0.76𝑧0.76z=0.76). Shrouded Milky Ways are detected out to 1.4 Gpc (z=0.35𝑧0.35z=0.35). Even a shrouded Magellanic Cloud-like galaxy with Lint=109​L⊙subscript𝐿intsuperscript109subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm int}=10^{9}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} is visible out to 250 Mpc. Blackboxes larger than 300 kpc in radius are visible just from the EBL heating alone.

Using equation 55, I find the reach of the 217 GHz PCCS2 catalog is about 27 million galaxies including 1.8×1018​M⊙1.8superscript1018subscriptMdirect-product1.8\times 10^{18}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} of stars with about 3×10183superscript10183\times 10^{18} terrestrial planets (1.2×10171.2superscript10171.2\times 10^{17} of them not orbiting M dwarfs). Even taking into account the possibility of statistical flukes, the PCCS2 is capable of setting an upper limit of about 1 blackbox per 7 million galaxies and per 5×1017​M⊙5superscript1017subscriptMdirect-product5\times 10^{17}\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} at 95% confidence level. There are essentially no improvements for shrouded galaxy clusters at z≤0.5𝑧0.5z\leq 0.5, because they would already have been detected at 70 to 143 GHz.

Whereas Planck covers most of the sky to low sensitivity, the SPT-SZ survey reaches much higher sensitivity over about two percent of the sky (Table 4). Within that sky region, its reach is truly enormous. This is seen in Figure 10, where the brightest blackboxes with 1013​L⊙superscript1013subscriptLdirect-product10^{13}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} are detected beyond 10 Gpc of comoving distance – at redshift 13, when the Universe was just 300 million years old. A trillion L⊙subscriptLdirect-product\textrm{L}_{\odot} blackbox is detectable out to 8 Gpc of comoving distance (z=4.7𝑧4.7z=4.7, at a cosmic age of 1.3 Gyr). The range for shrouded Milky Ways is 4.5 Gpc (z=1.5𝑧1.5z=1.5). SPT-SZ can see a shrouded Magellanic Cloud with Lblackbox≈109​L⊙subscript𝐿blackboxsuperscript109subscriptLdirect-productL_{\rm blackbox}\approx 10^{9}\ \textrm{L}_{\odot} out to 1 Gpc. For most of these galaxy types, the limiting factor is no longer the distance but the time it takes for starfaring entities to evolve. Further improvement on SPT-SZ for median-sized shrouded galaxies is better done with a larger sky area rather than a fainter flux sensitivity.

If I ignore the cosmological evolution of galaxies and starfarers, I find that the deeper flux limits roughly balances the smaller sky area compared to Planck. The 150 GHz band of the SPT-SZ survey can sample about 22 million galaxies with 0.8 quintillion M⊙subscriptMdirect-product\textrm{M}_{\odot} and 1.2 quintillion terrestrial planets.

Together, these two surveys have the capability to set incredible limits on cosmic engineers. Most of the galaxies in the SPT-SZ survey’s reach are further away than those that are within the reach of PCCS2, so if nothing is found in either, that rules out blackboxes in about 50 million galaxies with about 4 quintillion terrestrial planets (150 quadrillion not orbiting M dwarfs). The combined effective volume is around 10​Gpc310superscriptGpc310\ \textrm{Gpc}^{3}. In other words, Planck and the SPT can sample about 6% of the galaxies in the later half of the observable Universe’s history.

5. An Argument for Cosmic Pessimism

There have been a few attempts to reconcile the Fermi-Hart argument with the possibility of prevalent, long-lived starfarers. Following Grinspoon (2013), these scenarios might be called “Cosmic Optimism”. In this section, I interpret the null results for the blackbox search as evidence for the opposite scenario, Cosmic Pessimism. That is, there are no aliens in the local Universe, and we (and other societies) have a large chance of destroying ourselves, although starfaring is technologically possible. As with all interpretations of SETI results, support for Cosmic Pessimism involves a lot of subjective judgments and so should be regarded as suggestive rather than definitive.

5.1. We are (probably) alone

All useful searches for Type III societies are able to rule out trillions of planets as their potential birth sites. Waste heat is generally believed to be the most robust sign of massive engineering, as it is a consequence of thermodynamics, and thermodynamics suggests that the optimal temperature for many projects is around 3 K, the coldest possible without exotic physics. My search in the Planck source catalog for galactic-sized structures with 3 K waste heat instead rules out their existence among millions of galaxies. Furthermore, rich galaxy clusters shrouded in blackboxes simply do not exist within the observable Universe.

Even if one does not believe that Type III societies are motivated by thermodynamics, all other searches have found nothing. Perhaps waste heat from Type III societies is warmer, but Ĝ found no sign of them among about a hundred thousand galaxies in the WISE catalog. Or perhaps we could abandon the waste heat idea entirely. But as I pointed out in Lacki (2015), there are no signs of non-thermal emission from Type III societies either. The quietness of the cosmic radio background, for example, implies that less than 10−5superscript10510^{-5} of the Universe’s luminosity is converted into radio broadcasts. Similar constraints exist for gamma rays, neutrinos, low frequency gravity waves, and the highest energy cosmic rays. Nor are there signs of expanding, intergalactic Type III societies, which would have spread to the Milky Way by now if their abundances were much greater than my constraints (Olson, 2015). Finally, one could look for signs that they are moving stars and interstellar matter (Voros, 2014), or otherwise altering their galaxies’ appearance (Carrigan, 2012; Wright et al., 2014a). To my knowledge, there has not been a survey reported in the literature for artificial morphologies among many galaxies. But thousands of people working for the Galaxy Zoo program have examined the shapes of nearly a million galaxies and classified them. Users have identified new and unusual objects, like Hanny’s Voorwerp and Green Pea galaxies, but nothing artificial has been reported (Lintott et al., 2011). Arguably, the very fact that we are able to find empirical relations that apply to galaxies throughout the Universe hints that they are mostly governed by the same non-artificial processes. These results all imply that Type III societies are not present in the observable Universe.

If Type III societies do not exist, does that mean that societies like our own are rare? My own take is a provisional, cautious yes: we may in fact be alone in the observable Universe.777If we live in an infinite Universe, which at least seems plausible, then aliens almost certainly exist somewhere or somewhen, because we exist, implying the probability of technological societies emerging on any given planet is nonzero (as noted in Wesson 1990). When I say that we may be alone, I am referring to the observable Universe only.

The implications of the null result can be interpreted in the form of an altered Drake equation, which relates the number of societies with the number of planets, the chances of a society arising, and their lifespans:

NIII(ρSFR​Veff/⟨m⋆⟩)​np​fh=fl​fi​fc​fIII​ℒIII.subscript𝑁IIIsubscript𝜌SFRsubscript𝑉effdelimited-⟨⟩subscript𝑚⋆subscript𝑛𝑝subscript𝑓ℎsubscript𝑓𝑙subscript𝑓𝑖subscript𝑓𝑐subscript𝑓IIIsubscriptℒIII\frac{N_{\rm III}}{(\rho_{\rm SFR}V_{\rm eff}/\langle m_{\star}\rangle)n_{p}f_{h}}=f_{l}f_{i}f_{c}f_{\rm III}{\cal L}_{\rm III}. (58)

A survey finds NIIIsubscript𝑁IIIN_{\rm III} Type III societies in a volume Veffsubscript𝑉effV_{\rm eff} that includes many galaxies. The first term that limits this number is the rate that stars are formed in the volume, which can be found from the comoving cosmic star-formation rate ρSFRsubscript𝜌SFR\rho_{\rm SFR}, and the typical mass of a star, m⋆subscript𝑚⋆m_{\star}, which is about 0.35​M⊙0.35subscriptMdirect-product0.35\ \textrm{M}_{\odot} for the Chabrier IMF used by Baldry et al. (2012) (Draine, 2011). Further limiting factors are the number of planets per star (npsubscript𝑛𝑝n_{p}), the fraction of those planets that are habitable (fhsubscript𝑓ℎf_{h}), the probability that life appears on one of the habitable planets (flsubscript𝑓𝑙f_{l}), the probability that life evolves intelligent species (fisubscript𝑓𝑖f_{i}), and the probability that intelligence develops technology comparable to our own and possibly capable of interstellar communication (fcsubscript𝑓𝑐f_{c}). I have multiplied another factor fIIIsubscript𝑓IIIf_{\rm III}, the fraction of technological species that go on to become Type III societies. The limiting terms together multiply out to the rate at which Type III societies appear; at any given time, NIIIsubscript𝑁IIIN_{\rm III} is found by multiplying it with ℒIIIsubscriptℒIII{\cal L}_{\rm III}, the lifespan of the evidence for Type III societies or the age of the Universe, whichever is shorter. I have written the equation this way to emphasize that the null observation is being used to constrain the unknown factors on the right, rather than attempting to come up with NIIIsubscript𝑁IIIN_{\rm III} by estimating all of the factors.

Searches for the artifacts of starfarers are powerful because the relevant lifetime is not the lifetime of the society, but the lifetime of the artifacts (Carrigan, 2012). For example, many of the surfaces in the Solar System are billions of years old, and they all appear completely pristine. Some structures, like abandoned cities or strip mines, would be visible even after all of this time. The lack of these structures says something not just about the number of societies in the Galaxy today, but all societies that have ever lived in the past 4 Gyr. If flsubscript𝑓𝑙f_{l}, fisubscript𝑓𝑖f_{i}, and fcsubscript𝑓𝑐f_{c} are all around 0.1, this amounts to about a hundred million societies in the Milky Way alone (c.f., Freeman & Lampton, 1975). One reason Fermi’s Paradox is so powerful is that it bypasses ℒℒ{\cal L} in a way that searches for living societies don’t (but at the added cost of an unknown probability that societies become starfaring).

Galaxy-spanning Type III societies have a minimum lifespan of 100 kyr because of causality. In principle, they could survive for billions of years. Effective immortality may not be inevitable, but a blackbox may outlive its creators as a functioning ecosystem. Even without any kind of self-repair, the natural survival time of a dipole cloud with τabs=1subscript𝜏abs1\tau_{\rm abs}=1 is a fraction of a percent of the galaxy’s or cluster’s dynamical time: a few hundred kyr for a galaxy, and a few hundred Myr for a cluster (Appendix B). Thus, the null result implies

This confirms the need for some kind of “Great Filter”, some process that sets at least one of the remaining factors in equation 59 to nearly zero (Hanson, 1998; Bostrom, 2002). Without any further observational evidence, we have no reason to conclude that fIIIsubscript𝑓IIIf_{\rm III} must be zero. By symmetry, we might come up with a Bayesian prior that says it’s equally likely for any one of the four factors to be zero while the rest are one, for example.

This kind of argument depends on the grouping of the parameters; it matters whether fIIIsubscript𝑓IIIf_{\rm III} represents one threshold or many. Against the estimates of Carter, Livio (1999) disputed that humanity’s evolution timescale and the Sun’s lifetime are independent, while Ćirković et al. (2009) argued that short evolutionary timescales are possible because catastrophes can reset any evolutionary development.
